implementation_notes: Kotlin absorbs the concrete-factory part of the pattern: an `object` or a companion object is a language-level singleton that can implement the factory interface, so Material/Cupertino families need no manual singleton plumbing, and companion objects are the documented place for factory methods. A sealed interface closes the set of family implementations and makes `when` selection exhaustive, while DI (Hilt/Koin) or a `forPlatform` selector replaces the if/else chain. Keep product families as data classes or small interfaces so platform consistency stays checkable by the type system. For the invoke() operator pattern in a companion object, note that it makes the type look like a constructor call but DI frameworks do not automatically select or replace it; prefer an explicit factory method name in testable code.
pitfalls: object properties are initialized lazily on first access; expensive work in a factory object's initializer surfaces as a first-call stall, so keep initialization cheap or make it explicit.
A companion object named Factory next to a type that is itself a product invites confusion between the factory of that type and the family factory; use a distinct family name.
Global object factories cannot carry per-client configuration safely; keep mutable state out of them or use a class factory with constructor parameters and an explicit lifetime.

Using an invoke() operator in a companion hides family selection behind constructor-like syntax; DI registration and tests still need an explicit factory value, so prefer a named method when selection or substitution matters.
